newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel forces on high alert for guerrilla attacks.
newsitem.headline: Israel forces on high alert for guerrilla attacks.

text.p: Israel, fearing guerrilla vengeance attacks, went on high security alert on Wednesday ahead of the one-year anniversary of the assassination of a militant Islamic leader, officials and witnesses said.

"Israel police have bolstered their deployment to counter possible terrorist attacks...(police chief) Assaf Hefetz has ordered reinforcement of police forces in crowded areas, overt and covert patrols, roadblocks and thorough checks," a police spokeswoman said.

Fathi Shqaqi, slain leader of the militant Islamic Jihad group behind suicide attacks in Israel, was gunned down last October 26 in Malta. His assassins were never found but Israel's Mossad secret service is widely believed to be behind the killing.
Islamic Jihad has vowed to avenge his assassination.
Yigal Pressler, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's adviser on counter-terrorism, warned Israelis to be on alert for suspicious packages, people and cars.
Witnesses said Israeli sappers were positioned at major intersections in Jerusalem and special bomb-squad vehicles patrolled the city.

They said bomb squads closed streets and rushed pedestrians to side alleys while inspecting suspicious parcels. Israeli security forces and police trainees took up positions at bus stops along Jerusalem streets.
"The warning I issued stemmed from several reasons. One of them was the death of Islamic Jihad leader Shqaqi -- the first anniversary is on Saturday," Pressler told Israel radio.
"The second reason is that extremist elements might try to sabotage the Israeli-Palestinian negotiations by carrying out terror attacks," Pressler said.

Israel and the Palestinian Liberation Organisation are locked in marathon U.S.-mediated talks on a long-overdue Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron. The partial Hebron pullback, due last March, was delayed after a wave of Islamic suicide attacks killed 59 in Israel last February and March.
In self-ruled Gaza, lines of Palestinian trucks were backed up at a commercial checkpoint after Israel barred their entrance into the Jewish state.
"We stopped the movement of trucks from Karni checkpoint out of suspicion of attacks," Shlomo Dror, spokesman for Israel's policy chief for the West Bank and Gaza, told Reuters.
Dror said no restrictions were placed on Palestinian trucks in the West Bank and that Gazan labourers with valid work permits were not blocked from reaching jobs in Israel.
